blocks.en: Stripe just sent your server a charge.succeeded webhook.
Your pod was mid-restart. The webhook timed out. Stripe will retry — but now you're racing.
Here's the setup:

NestJS API on ECS, 4 tasks behind an ALB. Stripe POSTs charge.succeeded events to /webhooks/stripe. You have ~10s to return a 200 before Stripe times out and queues a retry. On Black Friday you're handling ~80 webhooks/sec.
Three failure modes are already happening in prod:
Pod restarts mid-deploy webhook missed Stripe retries you process it, but a second pod also→→→ processed the original →double charge confirmation email sent
DB is slow at peak handler takes 12s Stripe times out retries now you're processing the same→→→→ event twice while the first one is still running

Stripe sends charge.succeeded then charge.refunded 200ms apart your queue delivers them out of→ order you mark the order paid AFTER it was already refunded→ The handler is a 30-line function that does the right thing 99% of the time. The 1% is killing you.

Idempotency key + dedup table — store every event ID on receipt, skip if already seen. Retry with exponential backoff + dead-letter queue — never drop a webhook, process at-least- Verify signature, return 200 immediately, push to an internal queue — decouple receipt from Sequence numbers + reorder buffer — hold events until the prior sequence has landed, then What do you do? once. processing. process in strict order.
DAY 11 · ANSWERS & EXPLANATIONS Answer 1 CORRECT ANSWER
Answer: C — Verify signature, return 200 immediately, push to an internal queue ✅ Here's why, and why the other three trick smart engineers:
Why C wins (Sync receipt + async processing):
blocks.lead: Why C wins (Sync receipt + async processing)

blocks.en: The fundamental problem is that Stripe's clock and your handler's clock are decoupled. Stripe gives you ~10 seconds to ACK. Your DB write, your fraud check, your email send — none of that should live inside that 10-second window. Ever.

The pattern: validate the HMAC signature in <5ms, write the raw payload to SQS / Kafka / Redis Streams, return 200. Now your handler is bounded by network + signature verification, not by whatever your downstream services are doing today. Pod restart mid-processing? The message is already durable in the queue — a worker picks it up. DB slow? The webhook endpoint doesn't care — it returned 200 in 8ms. This is what Stripe, Shopify, and GitHub literally tell you to do in their own webhook docs.
Answer 2
Why A is the trap answer (Idempotency key + dedup table):
blocks.lead: Why A is the trap answer (Idempotency key + dedup table)

blocks.en: This is the answer that fools senior engineers in interviews — and it's not wrong, it's just incomplete.

Yes, you absolutely need idempotency. Stripe will deliver the same event ID more than once. A dedup table keyed on event.id with a unique constraint is table stakes. But it doesn't solve the original pain: the handler is still synchronous, still on the critical 10-second path, still getting killed by pod restarts mid-write.

If you ship A alone, you've prevented double-processing — but you're still timing out, still triggering retries, still creating the conditions for the race. Idempotency is a property your handler must have, not an architecture. C is the architecture; A lives inside it. The senior engineer trap is treating idempotency as the whole answer when it's one of three layers.
Answer 3
Why B is wrong as the answer (Retry + DLQ):
blocks.lead: Why B is wrong as the answer (Retry + DLQ)

blocks.en: Stripe is already doing the retry with exponential backoff. That's their job, not yours. Stripe retries failed webhooks for up to 3 days with backoff. You don't need to build that for inbound webhooks — you'd be duplicating provider behavior.

Retry + DLQ is the right pattern for your internal queue (the one C creates), not for the webhook endpoint itself. If your worker fails to process a queued event, sure, retry it and DLQ after N attempts.
But that's a downstream concern. Putting "retry logic" at the webhook receiver level confuses inbound and outbound retry semantics.
Answer 4
Why D is wrong (Sequence numbers + reorder buffer):
blocks.lead: Why D is wrong (Sequence numbers + reorder buffer)

blocks.en: This sounds rigorous and it's the answer engineers reach for after they've been burned by ordering once. The problem: most webhook providers don't give you sequence numbers. Stripe doesn't. GitHub doesn't. Even when they do (Shopify's X-Shopify-Webhook-Id), the gaps aren't dense — you can't tell "missing event 47" from "47 was filtered."

More importantly: ordering at the receiver is the wrong layer. You handle ordering at the domain level — when you process charge.refunded, you check the current state of the order before transitioning. If the order is already in refunded, you no-op. State machines beat reorder buffers because they handle the case where events arrive out of order AND the case where one of them never arrives at all. A reorder buffer just means you stall forever when an event gets dropped upstream.
